channel_name: No Priors · Elad Gil & Sarah Guo
video_title: Rethinking Legacy Data Infrastructure with Eon Co-Founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein
gist: Eon co-founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein argue that as models and compute commoditize, proprietary enterprise data becomes the last real moat, pointing to Google's $10M purchase of bankrupt Spirit Airlines' data as the leading edge of a land grab, while warning that AI agents with legitimate system access are creating an insider-threat-at-machine-speed security crisis that legacy data tooling and dashboards were never built to handle.

insights.claim: As models and compute become commoditized with near-zero switching cost, proprietary company data becomes the most valuable and durable asset a business owns.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Investors should weight data ownership/access moats over model or infra moats when evaluating AI-era enterprise value.
insights.quote: The most valuable thing that you have is actually your data.

insights.claim: Because AI tools are now broadly accessible to companies of any size, the competitive playing field has flattened, leaving people and proprietary data as the only real remaining advantages.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Undermines the assumption that AI itself is a durable differentiator; due diligence should focus on what proprietary data and talent a company actually controls.
insights.quote: the only real advantage that company have today is of course their people but also the data that they've approved because everyone has access to all of those cool new tools.

insights.claim: Enterprises are moving past indiscriminate token consumption toward demanding measurable value per token as usage costs scale.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Signals a maturing buyer market that will reward AI infra/data vendors who can prove ROI per token, not just raw usage volume.
insights.quote: we're not in the time of token maxing anymore

insights.claim: Google acquired Spirit Airlines' data (not its aircraft) out of bankruptcy for $10 million specifically to train and monetize AI models.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: A concrete, priced precedent for enterprise data being stripped out of distressed companies as an AI training asset, potentially reshaping bankruptcy asset valuation.
insights.quote: They didn't buy airplanes. They bought the data. They bought the data for $10 million because they think it's very important in that perspective.

insights.claim: The competing bidder against Google for Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy data was reportedly Mercor, indicating multiple AI-focused buyers actively competing for distressed enterprise datasets.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil (host)
insights.so_what: If accurate, shows AI data-labeling/training companies are now direct bidders in bankruptcy processes, a new and underappreciated category of M&A competitor.
insights.quote: I think the rumor too is that the other bidder on that data set was Merkor, right, in terms of the bankruptcy bid process.

insights.claim: Tech company CEOs are now routinely and unsolicited approached by buyers asking if they'll sell their company data, and AI labs are separately approaching Wall Street hedge funds to buy data for analyzing companies.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Suggests the Spirit Airlines deal is not a one-off but the visible edge of a broader emerging market for buying/leasing proprietary data assets across industries.
insights.quote: If you're a tech data CEO today I can tell you that you constantly get questions. Are you willing to sell your data?

themes.theme: Scarcity of Real-World Agent Training Data

insights.claim: High-quality, realistic (non-synthetic) datasets suitable for training enterprise agents remain scarce, which is why a newly released Harvard legal dataset stood out as notable.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Real enterprise data scarcity is a structural bottleneck for agent quality, creating demand and pricing power for firms holding authentic operational datasets.
insights.quote: you don't find too many good data sets that doesn't look like real synthetic data that can actually be used to really look like the real world

insights.claim: Datasets that capture how a real large enterprise actually functions (hierarchy, middle management, workers) are rare enough that companies actively ask what real internal data others have to train on.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Positions authentic multi-layered organizational data (like Spirit Airlines') as a distinct, hard-to-replicate training asset class beyond narrow domain datasets.

themes.theme: Why Legacy Data Stacks Break in the Agent Era

insights.claim: Established data tools (Fivetran, DBT, Monte Carlo) were built for single data teams pursuing narrow, predefined projects, and now fail because the business-unit owners who control data have incentives (uptime, security, compliance) misaligned with AI teams that want broad, unified access.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Explains why point-solution data tooling companies face disruption risk from new cross-org data foundation platforms like Eon.
insights.quote: Five was an incredible company, DBT and so on so forth, but very specific tools for that purpose.

insights.claim: Historically, data was collected and used for a single intended purpose, so unrelated datasets within the same company were never connected; the AI era rewards combining previously siloed datasets to answer entirely new questions.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Cross-dataset synthesis, not just single-source access, is the emerging value driver for enterprise data platforms.
insights.quote: Let's say that there's one person in organization who have all the list of all the people in New York who love burgers and another person in the organization have who has a database of all the people in New York who love pizza.

insights.claim: Enterprise data volumes are growing 'out of proportions,' driven heavily by AI agents themselves generating new data, producing both more value and more noise that requires new cleaning and classification tooling.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Agent-generated data growth is a new, largely unbudgeted infrastructure cost and data-quality problem for enterprises to manage.
insights.quote: The amount of data being ingested is absolutely insane especially comparing to earlier.

insights.claim: Databricks is responding to the agent-driven data explosion by building its own agents and databases to take charge of how data is created, rather than only cataloging data after the fact.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Signals incumbent data platforms are moving upstream into agent-native data creation, a competitive vector new entrants must account for.
insights.quote: if you can't beat them join them we'll build our own agents we'll build our own databases

themes.theme: AI Agents as the New Insider Threat

insights.claim: At AWS, a large disaster-recovery customer believed it was protected against ransomware but was not, because resources weren't properly mapped, classified, and tagged, resulting in 60% of the environment being exposed — the experience that motivated founding Eon.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Illustrates that data protection failures stem from poor classification/mapping, not just missing backup tech — a gap Eon is built to close.
insights.quote: 60% of the environment was uh was exposed by ransomware.

insights.claim: AI agents with legitimate system access now pose the same threat pattern as malicious human actors (e.g., dropping a database table), but the speed and scale at which it happens is far greater.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Enterprises must shift security posture to 'assume breach' from trusted, permissioned agents, not just external attackers — a new demand driver for data protection vendors.
insights.quote: What we're seeing now on steroids is that the same type of threat is coming from non-human actors, agents that essentially have legitimate access to the environment with legitimate permissions.

insights.claim: Enterprise sentiment on AI-agent security incidents flipped within months: virtually undiscussed six months ago, now nearly every company leader either fears such an incident or has personally experienced one.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: A fast-moving fear cycle like this typically precedes a wave of urgent security budget allocation — a timing signal for security/data-governance vendors.
insights.quote: six months ago, no, no one would even discuss with me. But a few months ago, pretty much every person I meet, every leader in a company tells me either they are afraid of that happening to them

insights.claim: Non-human identity (NHI) security has become one of the top problems in cybersecurity, evidenced by an explosion of startups building specifically for it.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: NHI security is a fast-growing, crowding investment category worth tracking for competitive differentiation and consolidation risk.
insights.quote: how many cyber security companies you see in in NHI in non identity right now an infinite amount and there's a reason for that it became number one number two problem right now

insights.claim: Non-technical employees are building apps and agent chains with no-code tools without understanding security or compliance implications, and their agents often invoke other agents, creating an ungoverned set of actors inside the organization handling sensitive data.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Shadow-AI proliferation from non-technical 'citizen builders' is an emerging governance blind spot distinct from traditional shadow IT, and a wedge for data-governance vendors.
insights.quote: So maybe their agent that they are building are using other agents and they're not technical to even understand what it means.

themes.theme: The Agentic Stack Still Needs Dashboards

insights.claim: Contrary to the assumption that agents replace dashboards, dashboards will proliferate because they become the primary way humans track what autonomous coding and other agents are doing, since agents now write most running code.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the narrative that BI/dashboard tooling gets disintermediated by agents — visibility/observability tooling may instead see rising demand.
insights.quote: I actually think we'll see more dashboards because this will be the only way to kind of figure out what they have going on in the world because first coding agent has started to write most of the code that's running in the wall.

insights.claim: The AI transformation is compressing enterprise adoption timelines far faster than the prior cloud migration wave, but the speed is causing customers to lose control to the point where fear of data leakage or IP loss is pausing adoption rather than accelerating it.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Loss-of-control anxiety is becoming a real adoption inhibitor, meaning vendors that can restore visibility/control (not just add AI capability) win enterprise trust and deals faster.
insights.quote: customers are losing control to a point where that's becoming an inhibitor, right? Not an enabler.

insights.claim: Unlike the cloud transition, which was abstract and hard to explain to non-technical stakeholders, everyone immediately understood AI's value after the ChatGPT moment, so adoption is being pushed by both genuine value and fear of falling behind.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Board/CEO-level FOMO is now a structural demand driver distinct from ROI-based buying, shortening sales cycles for AI vendors who can credibly promise fast deployment.
insights.quote: Cloud is basically just someone else's computer, but who knows what it is. It's hard to explain to my grandmother about the cloud AI. Everyone understands AI.

insights.claim: Forward-deployed-engineer go-to-market, once distinctive to Palantir, has become mainstream as legacy enterprises bring in outside engineers to implement AI faster than their own multi-year internal processes allow, compressing sales cycles.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: FDE motion is becoming a replicable GTM pattern across AI infra vendors, not a Palantir-specific moat — relevant for evaluating go-to-market strategy and margins of AI startups.
insights.quote: what's happening with forward deployed engineers used to be something look like services palenteer were doing that. No one really did understand what it means and now everyone's doing that.

insights.claim: Product-led growth, previously believed not to work for fragmented enterprise dev tools, is now being successfully combined with a forward-deployed-engineer motion (PLG for initial adoption, FDE to displace unwanted engineering work), as exemplified by Cognition.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: A hybrid PLG-plus-FDE playbook is emerging as the winning GTM template in AI infra, reversing prior conventional wisdom about PLG's limits in enterprise dev tools.
insights.quote: Now in the past I was arguing that for the majority of things PLG doesn't work especially for dev tools uh because the world is very fragmented

insights.claim: A new AI-driven roll-up thesis is emerging where firms like Long Lake acquire slow-moving legacy companies outright and transform them into AI-native operations for margin arbitrage, rather than selling AI tools to them.
insights.speaker: Eon co-founder
insights.so_what: Buy-and-transform roll-ups are a distinct, capital-intensive investment category betting on AI-driven margin expansion in legacy businesses, separate from selling software to them.
insights.quote: there are really great companies for example long lake that say instead of you adopting AI I know how to do it more efficiently. If I can buy the company and transform that into an AI company we can all win.
